title: Origins and Road to War
sub: Soviet collapse turns identity and language politics into a state crisis

markers.label: Chișinău
markers.description: Moldova's capital pushed language and sovereignty reforms that many east-bank industrial elites rejected.

markers.label: Tiraspol
markers.description: Tiraspol became the political center of the separatist Transnistrian project.

slides.title: A State Splits Along the Dniester
slides.cap: Visual reference for Origins and Road to War.
slides.body: The Transnistria War grew out of the Soviet collapse, Moldovan sovereignty politics, language laws, and the fears of Russian-speaking industrial communities east of the Dniester. Separatist leaders in Tiraspol claimed they were defending Soviet-era rights and local industry; Chișinău saw a challenge to the territorial integrity of the new Moldovan state.

stats.lbl: Conflict builds from sovereignty and language disputes.
The political break came before the main shooting war, so the map needs to show both capitals: Chișinău as the recognized state center and Tiraspol as the separatist center.

markers.label: Dubăsari
markers.description: Dubăsari saw early bloodshed and became one of the conflict's symbolic crossing points.

markers.label: Dniester crossings
markers.description: Bridges and crossings mattered because Transnistria's geography is a narrow strip along the river.

slides.title: The First Bloodshed
slides.body: Violence around Dubăsari showed that the political conflict could become armed confrontation. Control of bridges, police posts, and local institutions mattered because the Dniester was not only a river boundary; it was the line along which authority, identity, and security began to separate.

stats.lbl: Dubăsari turned constitutional argument into a security crisis and previewed the bridge-and-town geography of the 1992 war.

title: PMR State-Building and the 14th Army
sub: Separatist institutions grow beside Soviet military stockpiles

markers.label: Tiraspol
markers.description: The Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic built ministries, guards, and political institutions around Tiraspol.

markers.label: Cobasna depot
markers.description: Former Soviet ammunition and Russian military presence became a strategic shadow over the conflict.

slides.title: Institutions Before Recognition
slides.cap: Visual reference for PMR State-Building and the 14th Army.
slides.body: By 1991, Transnistrian separatists were not only protesting Moldovan policy; they were building parallel institutions. The Russian 14th Army and Soviet stockpiles did not automatically decide every clash, but their presence shaped everyone's calculations. Moldova faced a separatist region with weapons, factories, local guards, and a powerful external military factor.

stats.lbl: A separatist movement is much harder to reverse once it has armed guards, administrative offices, and access to former Soviet military infrastructure.

markers.label: Cocieri
markers.description: Moldovan police and local forces fought around Cocieri as the main armed phase opened.

markers.label: Dubăsari
markers.description: The Dubăsari area linked local clashes to the wider fight for control of the Dniester line.

slides.title: The Main War Opens
slides.cap: Visual reference for Cocieri and Dubăsari Fighting.
slides.body: The main armed phase began around Cocieri and Dubăsari in March 1992. Fighting involved Moldovan police, volunteers, Transnistrian guards, Cossacks, and former Soviet military networks. The battlefield was fragmented: villages, police stations, roadblocks, and bridges all carried political meaning.

stats.lbl: The conflict became a real war when local armed incidents linked into a sustained campaign along the Dniester.

title: Battle of Bender
sub: The bloodiest battle of the war

markers.label: Bender / Tighina
markers.description: Bender sits west of the Dniester but remained central to Transnistrian control, making it the war's most dangerous flashpoint.

markers.label: Dniester bridge
markers.description: The bridge linked Bender to Tiraspol and made urban fighting strategically decisive.

slides.title: Urban War at Bender
slides.cap: Visual reference for Battle of Bender.
slides.body: The Battle of Bender was the largest and bloodiest confrontation of the Transnistria War. Moldovan forces entered the city, Transnistrian forces counterattacked with support from Russian-linked elements, and civilians were trapped in urban fighting. The battle decided the war's military direction and made a negotiated ceasefire urgent.

stats.lbl: Bender made the conflict impossible to treat as a low-level separatist dispute; it was now an urban war with heavy civilian risk and outside military involvement.

markers.label: Tiraspol
markers.description: The 14th Army's role and Alexander Lebed's arrival changed the balance after Bender.

markers.label: Moscow
markers.description: The ceasefire was shaped through Russian-Moldovan diplomacy.

slides.title: A Ceasefire With Russian Weight Behind It
slides.cap: Visual reference for Lebed's Intervention and Ceasefire.
slides.body: After Bender, the Russian 14th Army's role became decisive in stopping Moldova from restoring control by force. The July 1992 ceasefire froze the separation line and created a peacekeeping arrangement. It ended the main war but preserved the unresolved political conflict.

stats.lbl: The ceasefire stopped the shooting but locked in a de facto statelet whose status remains unresolved.

markers.label: Bender
markers.description: Bender concentrated the civilian trauma of shelling, street fighting, and contested casualty narratives.

markers.label: Security Zone
markers.description: The postwar security zone became the physical expression of a frozen conflict.

slides.title: The Human Cost of a Frozen War
slides.cap: Visual reference for International and Human Dimensions.
slides.body: The war is usually described as killing roughly 1,000 people, with thousands more wounded or displaced. Bender concentrated much of that civilian trauma, while the postwar security zone turned the human cost into a long-term frozen-conflict reality.

stats.lbl: The war is usually described as killing roughly 1,000 people, with thousands more wounded or displaced. Bender concentrated much of that civilian trauma, while the postwar security zone turned the human cost into a long-term frozen-conflict reality.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: A short war creates a long frozen conflict

markers.label: Tiraspol
markers.description: Transnistria remained de facto separate after the ceasefire.

markers.label: Chișinău
markers.description: Moldova retained international recognition over the territory but not effective control.

slides.title: No Final Settlement
slides.cap: Bender remains one of the core memory sites of the war.
slides.body: The Transnistria War ended with a ceasefire, not reintegration. Transnistria became a de facto state backed by Russian military presence, while Moldova remained internationally recognized within its Soviet-era borders. The conflict became one of the defining frozen conflicts of the post-Soviet space.

stats.lbl: The front line hardened into a political reality that outlasted the war by decades.
